en: Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, together with a great saṅgha of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus and a multitude of bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

Then, indeed, the Blessed One—surrounded and honored by an assembly of many hundreds of thousands—was teaching the Dharma; he was fully revealing the holy life that is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end, excellent in meaning, excellent in phrasing, unique, complete, pure, and utterly refined.

Now at that time, King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha, having departed from the great city of Rājagṛha with great royal splendor and great royal majesty, approached the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, where the Blessed One was staying. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha said this to the Blessed One:

“Blessed One, how does there come to be a re-manifestation of the mind at the time of death when an action that has been performed and accumulated has long since ceased? Or, how is it known that actions do not perish, given that all conditioned phenomena are empty? When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śreṇya Bimbisāra, the King of Magadha:

"It is just as if, O Great King, a man who was asleep were to enjoy the company of a woman, the most beautiful in the land, within a dream. Having woken from his sleep, he would recollect that woman, the most beautiful in the land. What do you think, O Great King? Does that woman, the most beautiful in the land, exist within the dream? The King replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Great King? Would that man be considered wise who, having enjoyed the most beautiful woman of the land in a dream, would then recall her and experience a thrill of passion for her? The King said, "Certainly not, Blessed One. And why is that? Because, Blessed One, in a dream the most beautiful woman of the land does not exist and is not to be found in the ultimate sense. How much less, then, could there be any enjoyment of her? That man would only be a partaker of frustration and exhaustion."

The Blessed One said: "In the same way, Great King, an ignorant, unlearned worldling, having seen forms with the eye, becomes attached to those things that are grounds for joy or dejection. Being attached, he is drawn toward them; being drawn toward them, he becomes impassioned. Being impassioned, he performs actions born of passion, hatred, and delusion through body, speech, and mind. And that performed action ceases within the mind."

As it ceases, it does not remain dependent upon the eastern direction, nor the southern, nor the western, nor the northern, nor above, nor below, nor any intermediate direction. Eventually, when the time of death has arrived and the final consciousness is in the process of ceasing due to the exhaustion of its corresponding karma, that karma becomes manifest to the mind, just as a man who has just woken from sleep might think of a woman who is the most beautiful in the land.

Thus indeed, O Great King, the consciousness of the final existence ceases, and the consciousness of the first moment pertaining to rebirth arises—whether among the gods, or among humans, or among asuras, or in the hells, or among animals, or among the hungry ghosts.

And, O Great King, immediately upon the manifestation of that first consciousness which belongs to the portion of rebirth, there proceeds a stream of mind (cittasaṃtati) of a similar nature, wherein the experience of the maturation (vipāka) of karmas is discerned. In this regard, O Great King, no dharma whatsoever transmigrates from this world to the next world; yet both death and rebirth are discerned.

In this regard, Great King, that which is the cessation of the final consciousness is death; that which is the manifestation of the first consciousness is birth. In this regard, Great King, the final consciousness, when ceasing, does not go anywhere; the first consciousness, pertaining to rebirth, when arising, does not come from anywhere. Why is that? Because all phenomena are by nature secluded.

In this regard, Great King, the final consciousness is empty of the final consciousness; death is empty of death; the initial consciousness is empty of the initial consciousness; and rebirth is empty of rebirth. Yet, the non-perishing of karmic actions is discerned.

And for that initial consciousness belonging to the stage of rebirth, Great King, which has just arisen immediately after [death], there proceeds a continuous stream of mind (cittasaṃtati) that is homogeneous and unwavering, wherein the experience of the maturation of karmic actions is discerned.
Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, then further said this:
"All this is mere name, established in mere designation. Apart from the expression, the expressed object does not exist. [1]

For by whatever name each phenomenon is expressed, that phenomenon does not exist therein; for such is the true nature of phenomena. Indeed, the state of being a name is empty of a name, and within a name, no name is found.
All phenomena are nameless, yet they are fully described by means of names.
For these phenomena are unreal, having arisen from conceptual construction;
even that conceptual construction by which emptiness is conceptualized does not exist here.
That which was spoken by the Seer of Reality— that one sees form with the eye—
is presented as true only by way of worldly convention for those who possess false conceit.
Wherever the Leader reveals vision within the totality of conditions,
the wise one [reveals] the cognition of ultimate reality as residing on the level of metaphorical designation. [6]
[The Buddha said: "What is the supreme truth? The eye does not see form, nor does the mind perceive phenomena. This indeed is the supreme truth, wherein the world does not penetrate. [7]

Thus spoke the Blessed One. King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha, filled with joy, as well as those monks, those bodhisattvas, and that entire assembly—including the world of gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas—rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. The thirteenth Mahāyāna sūtra, titled *Bhavasaṃkrānti*, is complete.
